pinboard.title: Introducing K2 Horizon: Frontier Performance, Radically Open ( September 3, 2026 - Institute of Foundation Models)
pinboard.description:
Explore K2 Horizon, IFM’s open-source fleet of six frontier AI models for reasoning, coding, agentic workflows, edge devices, and enterprise deployment.




Artifacts

Socials
K2 Horizon mountain artwork at sunset

    Overview
    Performance
    The fleet
    Designing Horizon
    Open science
    Get started
    Full results

Today IFM is releasing K2 Horizon, a connected fleet of six models: 375B-A23B, 36B-A4B, 32B, 7B, 3.7B, and 0.9B. Across reasoning, mathematics, coding, agentic tasks, and general capabilities, K2 Horizon delivers top-tier performance in every size class—with the 0.9B, 3.7B, and 7B models setting new state of the art at their respective scales.

K2 Horizon is also our most comprehensive open release to date. For every model, we are opening the training lifecycle from pretraining through reasoning and agentic post-training. We are releasing intermediate checkpoints, training data or detailed data-construction recipes, open architecture, mixture compositions, training code, configurations, fine-grained logs, evaluation results, and final weights.

The models and code are released under the Apache 2.0 license. Datasets are released under their applicable licenses, such as ODC-BY; We disclose how the data was constructed and mixed when redistribution is not possible.

Together, K2 Horizon represents the most comprehensive open model release to date:

    A new performance frontier across scales.
    The 0.9B, 3.7B, and 7B models achieve world-leading performance in their size classes across widely used evaluations. The 36B-A4B model, equipped with our new Mixture-of-Value-Attention (MoVA) mechanism, delivers exceptional capability per active parameter, outperforming some much larger models. The 32B and 375B-A23B models rank among the top models in their respective classes. Together, the six models provide competitive performance across deployment environments ranging from edge devices to the enterprise.
    The first fully open model fleet for agents.
    K2 Horizon is the first open model family to expose the complete development process through agentic post-training. By releasing checkpoints, data (or data recipe), code, configurations, and training logs across every stage, K2 Horizon makes it possible to study how reasoning, tool use, planning, and agentic capabilities emerge; reproduce the methods that create them; and adapt those methods to new tools, environments, and domains.
    Six models spanning edge to enterprise.
    The 0.9B model is designed for highly constrained environments such as watches and glasses, while the 3.7B and 7B models bring advanced capabilities to phones and other on-device applications. The dense 32B model and sparse 36B-A4B model provide powerful options for local workstations and efficient serving. The 375B-A23B model brings the fleet’s strongest capabilities to demanding enterprise deployments. All six models include quantization support.
    One connected fleet.
    The six models share core architecture, vocabulary, training methodology, interfaces, evaluation infras

pinboard.title: Healthcare organizations can now connect EHR and additional industry data to ChatGPT
pinboard.description:
ChatGPT can now connect to trusted healthcare data, helping clinicians securely access patient context, medical research, and more.

Healthcare organizations need AI that works across the systems and information central to care and operations. Patient context, medical evidence, public healthcare data, and organizational knowledge often live in different places. Connecting these sources in a governed workspace helps teams find the right information, understand it in context, and put it to work across the business.

Today, we’re introducing a new electronic health record integration that brings authorized patient context from Epic into ChatGPT for Healthcare, along with the Healthcare Public Data plugin for direct, structured access to official healthcare datasets like PubMed, DailyMed, and CMS Coverage. Together, these capabilities bring ChatGPT closer to the systems and sources healthcare teams trust, while supporting the controls and compliance healthcare work requires.
Bring ChatGPT and EHR context together

Healthcare organizations can now connect Epic environments to ChatGPT. Instead of searching across appointment notes, laboratory results, medications, and specialist documentation, clinicians can ask:

    What has changed since this patient’s last visit?
    Which recent lab results should I review before today’s appointment?
    Have there been medication changes or new specialist recommendations?
    What follow-ups, referrals, or unresolved issues should I be aware of?

Wendell Berry's Eternal Story - First Things
pinboard.description:
"Ten years ago, an editor at Penguin approached me to ask if I would like to edit a collection of essays by Wendell Berry for a British audience. Berry’s essays had never been published in book form in the U.K.; the editor had only recently discovered his writing and decided to remedy that deficit. He approached me because an internet search had turned up an essay of mine about Berry. Not too many British people, then as now, knew his name or wrote about him. I hope that will change now. Wendell Berry’s principal literary talent, according to his own wife, Tanya, was “to repeat himself for seventy years.” This observation was intended as a compliment rather than a criticism, and understanding why that might be is perhaps the key to understanding Berry. Often presented as a straightforward “southern agrarian” writer, or as a holdover from another time, he was a good deal more complex than either of these labels might suggest. For a start, Berry was not a “simple farmer” who had never left his homeplace. He was a writer, with a writer’s mind, who had initially set out for New York City in the 1960s to work on his literary ambitions. Only on arriving did he come to see that the city had no stories for him; that his work, in fact, was to tell the stories of the place he had left behind in small-town Kentucky. The story that Berry told and re-told for so long was the story of the decline of the human-scale world he grew up in, its replacement by a world of technology and bureaucracy, and the need to restore the human spirit again before it is too late. By rooting himself in one place and calling it home, Berry found what he needed to become the writer he wanted to be. In looking to the past—his own, and his land’s—he found the materials he needed to write about the present and its endless attacks on the things he valued, whether those attacks came in the form of mountaintop removal coal mining or from the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s war on small farmers, in the service of the agribusiness lobbies that had purchased it wholesale. Berry, though, like any true writer—really, like any honest human—did not easily find a simple contentment in the life he had chosen. He had to work for it. His poem “The Want of Peace” explores the tension that he must have felt as he plowed his land with draft horses and continued writing with pencil and paper, even as the tyranny of the silicon chip enveloped the world around him:
All goes back to the earth, and so I do not desire pride of excess or power, but the contentments made by men who have had little: the fisherman’s silence receiving the river’s grace, the gardener’s musing on rows.
This sounds nice, even platitudinous. But note that Berry “desires” this contentment: He does not claim to have found it, at least not yet, or not all of the time. In the second verse, he is quite open about the gap between desire and attainment:
I lack the peace of simple things. I am never wholly in place. I find no peace or grace. We sell the world to buy fire, our way lighted by burning men, and that has bent my mind and made me think of darkness and wish for the dumb life of roots.
The quest for the simple life doesn’t come easily for any of us in the age of runaway technology, and Berry’s novels, poems, and essays all delve into that same tension. He was always an activist as well as a writer, and his activism was grounded in the eternal things that he stood for: the land, his local community, his faith, his family. None of these became flags for him to wave, or weapons he used to attack others. All of them were employed instead with keen passion in opposition to the thing he always stood against: the modern monoculture, which destroyed small farms and small towns from Kentucky to Kerala to make way for the globalized blandishments of “free” market capitalism—the extractive corporate economy, which “sell[s] the world to buy fire.” Berry’s struggle, in other words, was a particular manifestation of a universal battle. This explains, perhaps, why people like myself, a boy from the English suburbs with no knowledge of farming, would find a kindred soul in his writings. I first came across Berry’s work as a young environmental writer and activist back in the 1990s, and though I could not have found Kentucky on a map (and probably still can’t), I found in this writer a calm yet passionate moral certainty that I lacked myself, because I had no grounding in any of the places it came from. That moral certainty is perhaps the keenest taste left by Berry’s multitudinous writings. It was never self-righteous—Berry was often self-deprecating, self-questioning, or drily funny—and neither did it pretend that “going back to the past” was any kind of easy solution to the complex mess of the present. His enemies liked to pretend that both of these things were true, but what they probably disliked most about him was that he actually practiced what he preached. Berry never bought a computer or used a smartphone; he wouldn’t use air travel; and he lived and worked in the small rural community he brought to life with his words. Unable to call him a hypocrite, his critics had to content themselves instead with calling him an unrealistic fossil, wedded to a dead past. But there was nothing simple about Wendell Berry, and he was not committed to some Romantic fantasy. He was committed to real human lives and real human work, in real, living communities. The ongoing destruction of all of these things was the fire lit under his words. Berry always saw in humanity’s relationship with its land, and with the wider creation, a litmus test of what kind of people we were, or were becoming. “I have made myself its follower and its apprentice,” he wrote of his own farm in his 1968 essay “A Native Hill.” If we wanted to begin living better lives, he wrote in 2011, we should also apprentice ourselves to something local and particular, in whatever form we found it. “We must not work or think on a heroic scale,” he insisted, because heroes “too lightly risk the lives of people, places, and things they do not see.” Instead, “we must work on a scale proper to our limited abilities. We must not break things we cannot fix.” A better world would not come through more grand plans, tech fixes, or centralized, ideological impositions. It would not come through “wage slavery or by enslaving nature.” It would come from the place it had always come from: “locally adapted economies, based on local nature, local sunlight, local intelligence, and local work.” In those few proposals, we can see both Wendell Berry’s prophetic genius and the reason he was so widely ignored by those with influence and power. Both of these legacies, I’m sure, will continue for a while. In the end, though, Berry will be proven right. Perhaps it will take the tragedy of collapse and overreach before we come to our senses. We must hope otherwise, but the signs do not look good. In the meantime, Wendell Berry’s beautiful poems, questing novels, and steadily passionate essays offer us all a legacy we can engage with. Those of us who are more flawed as human beings than he undoubtedly was, or less able to practice what we preach, can find a way in through the many doorways he built with words, backed up by decades of energetic practice. May he rest in peace."

How "ghost creators" cashed in on America’s divided politics • Semafor
pinboard.description:
Max Tani:

“William,” a middle-aged man in a blue short-sleeved button-down shirt whose YouTube videos have more than 14 million views, looked straight into the camera at his kitchen table in August and read a script about New York City’s mayor. His video, Mayor Mamdani Panics as Taylor Swift Triggers a $2.3 Billion Celebrity Exodus, quickly racked up more than 474,000 views. “Omar,” a shaggy, bearded creator who claimed to be based in New York, read a report to viewers in June about Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and her ex. AOC FREAKS OUT as Riley Roberts CAUGHT Running Her ENTIRE Operation, set to ominous music, got more than 250,000 views. The same music played on a video, Socialist Seattle Mayor CRIES As A Beloved Bookstore Closes, from a channel called Julian News Report. It also registered a quarter of a million views. To the casual YouTube viewer, these would look like unconnected videos from political news creators outraged by events happening in cities led by Democrats. The reality is more complicated. “William” and “Omar” are actors, Semafor found in a forensic accounting of their channels’ origins. They were reading formulaic, repetitive scripts that appeared to be generated or aided by large-language models. Over the last several months, a new generation of YouTube growth-hackers have flooded American politics with sensationalized, low-quality content, reaching millions of viewers with nearly identical videos taking aim at progressive politicians including Zohran Mamdani, California Gov. Gavin Newsom, and Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker. Notably, while the videos are presented as laypeople giving straight-to-camera ideological news recaps, they feature actors and spokespeople paid small amounts of money to read nearly identical scripts laced with misleading claims and outright falsehoods. Viewers either didn’t notice or didn’t mind: A single network of interconnected videos that are affiliated with a growth-hacking company whose founder promises to be the “strongest alternative to paid ads” garnered well over 45 million views and 90,000 comments on YouTube as well as millions more impressions across social platforms like TikTok. With that level of viral videos, a small media organization can make tens or even hundreds of thousands a month.

Marina Hyde mentioned a theory that all algorithmic feeds are fake these days. This feels like more confirmation of that.
